name: Memory-safety vulnerability identification and exploit construction
theory_paragraphs: A \term{memory-safety violation} occurs when a program reads or writes outside the memory region an object legitimately occupies. The course lists four possible consequences: \imp{data corruption, unexpected transfer of control, access violation, attacker-chosen code execution}. The process address space is divided into code and linked libraries, global data, the \term{heap} (dynamic allocations via \texttt{malloc}), and the \term{stack}. On a downward-growing stack, a frame holds from high to low addresses: function arguments, the \term{saved return address}, the \term{saved frame pointer}, then local variables. Pointers are 4 or 8 bytes; x86 stores multibyte values \term{little-endian}, so the address \texttt{0x4012b0} is embedded in a payload as the byte sequence $\texttt{b0}\,\texttt{12}\,\texttt{40}\,\texttt{00}$.

Recurring bug classes: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{Buffer overflow}: more data written than capacity --- \texttt{gets}, \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{strcat}, \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{scanf}/\texttt{fscanf} with \%s, \texttt{memcpy} with an unchecked length. \item \term{Buffer over-read}: more data read than capacity, e.g. \texttt{strcat} on an uninitialized buffer scans out of bounds for the terminating NUL byte (Heartbleed is the famous case); leaks adjacent secrets. \item \term{Dangling pointer / use-after-free}: pointer used after \texttt{free} or after its frame is destroyed; reallocation lets attacker-controlled bytes be reinterpreted as the old object. \item \term{Type confusion}: a wrong cast reinterprets an object (a \texttt{Dog*} used as a \texttt{Cat*}). \item \term{Uninitialized memory}: a fresh local may expose values left behind by earlier frames. \item \term{Double free / memory leak}: corrupts allocator metadata or exhausts memory. \end{tightitem}

Three escalation levels for a stack buffer overflow. (i) \term{Adjacent-local overwrite}: bytes just past the buffer land in a neighbouring local (an authentication flag or a data pointer), changing program logic without touching control data --- often the shortest attack, and the one students forget. (ii) \term{Return-address hijack}: fill the buffer and saved frame pointer, then overwrite the saved return address; on \texttt{return} the CPU jumps to the attacker-chosen address, e.g. an existing function whose address is known (\term{code reuse}; \term{return-oriented programming} chains \term{gadgets} --- short existing instruction sequences ending in an indirect jump --- to compute arbitrary operations without injecting any code). (iii) \term{Shellcode injection}: attacker-supplied machine code placed inside the overflowed buffer, with the return address pointed back into the buffer. Shellcode must be position-independent, contain no NUL bytes, and marshal its own syscall arguments (e.g. \texttt{execve} on \texttt{/bin/sh}); it requires \imp{an executable region and a known buffer address}.

Defenses and precisely which attack each one misses: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{Stack canary}: random per-execution value placed between the locals and the saved frame pointer, checked just before return; stops return-address overwrites but \imp{not adjacent-local corruption} --- the hijack of a flag or pointer happens before the check. \item \term{NX / W$\oplus$X}: no page is both writable and executable; stops injected shellcode but \imp{not jumps to existing code} (ret2func, ret2libc, ROP). \item \term{ASLR}: randomizes base addresses; stack-only ASLR preserves relative offsets within the stack and leaves code and heap addresses predictable, so heap-resident payloads and jumps to fixed code addresses survive. \item \term{Guard pages}: unmapped pages between regions trap a linear overflow that crosses them; useless for an overflow within a single frame. \item \term{Shadow stack / CFI}: a separate protected copy of return addresses, or hardware/software restriction of indirect targets. \item \term{Safe languages and bounded APIs}: \texttt{fgets}, \texttt{strncpy}, \texttt{snprintf}, explicit length checks; strong typing (Rust ownership, GC languages) removes the whole bug class at the cost of performance. \end{tightitem}
theory_cheatsheet: Frame layout (high $\rightarrow$ low): args, saved return address, saved frame pointer, locals; padding to reach the return address $=$ buffer size $+$ bytes of intervening locals $+$ saved FP.
Payload for a return hijack: filler bytes followed by the target address written little-endian.
Canary is checked only at return: it does \imp{not} protect flags or pointers overwritten earlier in the frame.
NX/W$\oplus$X stops injected shellcode only; jumping to existing functions (ret2func, ret2libc, ROP) still works.
Shellcode must be position-independent and NUL-free; it needs an executable region and a known buffer address.
Fix pattern: bounded copy (\texttt{fgets}/\texttt{strncpy}/\texttt{snprintf}), explicit check $\texttt{len} \leq \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$, initialize buffers, prefer a memory-safe language.
identify_givens: A short C program (5--15 lines) with attacker-controlled input (a \texttt{char*} from argv/stdin/file plus possibly an attacker-chosen length), containing a fixed-size stack buffer and/or a heap allocation, and one or more unsafe calls: \texttt{gets}, \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{strcat}, \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{fscanf} \%s, or \texttt{memcpy} with an unchecked length. The problem often states the stack layout (grows down, order of locals, pointer size), mentions an existing target function (e.g. a privileged routine at a known address) or a flag variable, and later sub-questions name defenses: stack canary, NX/W$\oplus$X, ASLR (stack base only vs full), guard pages.
identify_target: Identify the vulnerable lines and say why they are unsafe; construct a concrete attacker input that corrupts an adjacent local (flag/pointer), overwrites the saved return address to reach an existing function, or injects shellcode (stating assumptions about executability and known addresses); then judge for each named defense whether it stops each attack and why, and propose a working countermeasure for any attack that survives.
strategy_name: Trace the overflow into the layout, then match each defense to the attack it misses

algorithm.detail: Scan for unbounded copies: \begin{tightitem} \item \texttt{gets}, \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{strcat}, \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{scanf}/\texttt{fscanf} \%s into a fixed buffer; \item \texttt{memcpy(dst, src, len)} with attacker-controlled $\texttt{len} > \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$; \item \texttt{strcat}/\texttt{strlen} on an uninitialized buffer (out-of-bounds read hunting for the NUL byte); \item pointer used after \texttt{free}, type-confusing casts, double free. \end{tightitem} State for each flagged line \emph{which} memory region (stack/heap/global) it endangers.

Write down the relevant region in address order using the stated conventions. Stack growing down: arguments, saved return address, saved frame pointer, then locals; record exact byte counts and the pointer size (4 or 8 bytes). Confirm which local sits adjacent to the overflowable buffer --- \imp{the layout decides which attack is shortest}. For heap bugs, note the allocation size and what object or metadata follows it.

Choose the weakest point: \begin{tightitem} \item an adjacent local: flip an auth flag to nonzero, or retarget a data pointer so a later \texttt{strcmp} or write uses attacker bytes; \item the saved return address, reached with $\texttt{buffer\_size} + \texttt{intervening\_locals} + \texttt{sizeof(saved\_fp)}$ bytes of padding; \item heap metadata or an adjacent heap object; \item a dangling pointer via use-after-free. \end{tightitem}

Express the payload as a byte-count formula plus concrete bytes. Flag flip: $\texttt{sizeof(buffer)} + 1$ bytes with a nonzero last byte lands in the adjacent \texttt{int}. Return hijack: padding up to the saved return address, then the target address (e.g. the existing privileged function) in \term{little-endian} order, plus optional extra words that the target will read as arguments. Pointer retargeting: filler, then the address of the attacker's own buffer.

State the required assumption explicitly (\imp{executable stack or heap}). Place machine code (shellcode: position-independent, NUL-free, sets up \texttt{execve}) inside the attacker-controlled buffer, overwrite the saved return address with the buffer's own address, and on return the CPU jumps into the shellcode. State what you assume about knowing the buffer address (debugger, leaked pointer, no ASLR).

algorithm.action: Match each defense to the attack it misses
algorithm.detail: Evaluate per defense, per attack: \begin{tightitem} \item stack canary (checked just before return): stops return-address overwrites, not adjacent-local corruption --- the hijack happens before the check; \item NX/W$\oplus$X: stops injected shellcode, not jumps to existing functions (ret2func/ROP); \item stack-base ASLR: hides stack addresses but preserves relative offsets and leaves heap/code addresses known --- a heap-resident payload or fixed code target survives; full ASLR also randomizes libraries; \item guard pages: trap linear overflows crossing a region boundary, useless within a single frame. \end{tightitem}

Replace unsafe calls with bounded APIs (\texttt{fgets}, \texttt{strncpy}, \texttt{strncat}, \texttt{snprintf}, or an explicit check $\texttt{len} \leq \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$), initialize buffers before use, free once and NULL the pointer, add a canary for return-address protection, and prefer a memory-safe language. For each fix, name the original attack it kills.

variations.name: Adjacent local overwrite instead of return address
variations.detail: Some sittings ask for an input (other than the correct password) that makes the program take a privileged path; the shortest answer overflows a small buffer by one nonzero byte into an adjacent \texttt{int} auth flag --- no return address needed. Trap: students only write the classic return-address smash and miss the shorter attack. A second variant retargets an adjacent \texttt{char*} so a later \texttt{strcmp(input, input)} trivially succeeds. Canaries stop neither, because the corruption happens before the canary check at return.

variations.name: Heap overflow mixed with uninitialized-buffer over-read
variations.detail: One reexam mixes \texttt{memcpy(tmp, input, len)} with $\texttt{len} > 32$ (heap overflow), a stack overflow, and \texttt{strcat} on an uninitialized \texttt{buffer[32]} (out-of-bounds read while searching for the NUL byte). Adapt by analyzing each line separately and naming the affected region per line. Trap: forgetting that an uninitialized buffer has no NUL terminator, so the over-read occurs before any copying.

variations.name: Defense quiz with scope reversal (stack ASLR vs heap payload)
variations.detail: Per-defense verdicts with a scope trap: randomizing only the stack base defeats a jump to a stack-resident shellcode buffer but \emph{not} the same payload placed on the heap at a known address --- stack randomization does not move the heap. Guard pages do not stop an intra-frame stack overflow but can detect a heap overflow past a buffer if placed between heap regions. For every defense, ask \imp{which memory region it actually protects}.

variations.name: Shellcode vs return-to-existing-function
variations.detail: Some sittings provide an existing target function so no injection is needed (jump to its known address); others demand injected code, which requires stating the executable-stack assumption and a known buffer address. Notation traps: the pointer size (4 vs 8 bytes) changes the padding length, and little-endian byte order matters when writing the address into the input.

original_problem: A packet-processing daemon contains an existing function \texttt{spawn\_console} at address \texttt{0x4011c8} that opens a privileged console. The code below is not memory safe (\texttt{packet} and \texttt{plen} are attacker-controlled, pointers are 8 bytes; the chunk returned by \texttt{malloc} stores \texttt{user} at offset 0 and the 8-byte function pointer \texttt{on\_done} at offset 16; the stack grows down, and within the frame of \texttt{dispatch} the buffer \texttt{cmd} is the lowest local, with the saved frame pointer and the saved return address directly above it): \texttt{struct session \{ char user[16]; void (*on\_done)(void); \}; void enroll(char *packet, unsigned plen) \{ struct session *s = malloc(sizeof(struct session)); s->on\_done = log\_close; memcpy(s->user, packet, plen); /* Line A */ s->on\_done(); /* Line B */ \} void dispatch(char *packet, unsigned plen) \{ char cmd[24]; memcpy(cmd, packet, plen); /* Line C */ exec\_cmd(cmd); /* Line D: unknown commands are ignored */ \}} (a) Identify the vulnerable line(s) and explain why they are unsafe. (b) Give a value of \texttt{plen} and an input to \texttt{enroll} that makes the daemon execute \texttt{spawn\_console}, without touching any return address. (c) Give a value of \texttt{plen} and an input to \texttt{dispatch} that redirects execution to \texttt{spawn\_console} when \texttt{dispatch} returns, stating your byte layout and endianness. (d) Explain how the attacker could instead run injected code via \texttt{dispatch}, stating the required assumptions. (e) Does a stack canary stop attack (b)? Attack (c)? (f) Does NX (W$\oplus$X) stop attack (d)? (g) Which of attacks (b), (c), (d) survive if only the stack base is randomized? (h) Propose a countermeasure that fixes the root cause.

original_steps.work: Line A: \texttt{memcpy(s->user, packet, plen)} copies attacker-controlled bytes into the 16-byte heap field with an unchecked length --- a heap (intra-object) overflow that reaches \texttt{on\_done}. Line C: \texttt{memcpy(cmd, packet, plen)} does the same into the 24-byte stack buffer --- a stack buffer overflow. Line B is not itself a memory error but is the escalation point: it calls whatever pointer the overflow installed. Line D is benign. Note that unlike \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{memcpy} copies NUL bytes, so addresses containing \texttt{0x00} are delivered intact.

Heap chunk of \texttt{s}: \texttt{user} at offset 0 (16 bytes), \texttt{on\_done} at offset 16 (8 bytes). Frame of \texttt{dispatch} from high to low addresses: saved return address (8 bytes), saved frame pointer (8 bytes), \texttt{cmd[24]}. Array writes proceed toward higher addresses, so overflowing \texttt{cmd} reaches the saved frame pointer first, then the saved return address.

Attack (b) targets \texttt{on\_done}, $16$ bytes past the start of \texttt{user} --- no return address involved, and the hijack fires at the indirect call in Line B. Attack (c) targets the saved return address, $24 + 8 = 32$ bytes past the start of \texttt{cmd}.

Attack (b): $\texttt{plen} = 24$; input $=$ 16 filler bytes (\texttt{A}$\times 16$) followed by the 8-byte little-endian encoding of \texttt{0x4011c8}, i.e. $\texttt{c8}\,\texttt{11}\,\texttt{40}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}$. The first 16 bytes fill \texttt{user}; the next 8 overwrite \texttt{on\_done}, so Line B executes \texttt{spawn\_console()}. The five NUL bytes in the address survive because \texttt{memcpy} does not stop at \texttt{0x00} --- a string-based copy would truncate this payload.

Attack (c): $\texttt{plen} = 40$; input $=$ 32 filler bytes $+$ the 8-byte little-endian encoding of \texttt{0x4011c8} (40 bytes total: \texttt{A}$\times 32$ then $\texttt{c8}\,\texttt{11}\,\texttt{40}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}$). The filler covers \texttt{cmd} (24 bytes) and the saved frame pointer (8 bytes); the final 8 bytes overwrite the saved return address, so when \texttt{dispatch} returns the CPU jumps to \texttt{spawn\_console}. Delivery through \texttt{memcpy} is exactly why the zero bytes in the address cause no problem here.

Attack (d): assume the stack is executable and the address of \texttt{cmd} is known (no ASLR or a leaked pointer). Put position-independent machine code at the start of \texttt{packet} (\texttt{memcpy} even tolerates NUL bytes inside it, unlike string-copy delivery), pad with filler to 32 bytes, append the little-endian address of \texttt{cmd}, and set \texttt{plen} to the total length; on return, execution enters the injected code. Defense verdicts: (e) the canary sits between \texttt{cmd} and the saved frame pointer and is checked just before return --- it stops attack (c), but \emph{not} attack (b): \texttt{s} lives on the heap, no stack canary guards it, and the hijack fires at the indirect call before any return. (f) NX/W$\oplus$X stops attack (d) (the stack is no longer executable) but not (b) or (c), which jump to existing code. (g) Stack-base-only ASLR defeats attack (d) as stated (the address of \texttt{cmd} becomes unknown) but neither (b) nor (c): neither the heap chunk nor the code address \texttt{0x4011c8} is moved by stack randomization.

Fix (h): validate the length before each copy, e.g. \texttt{if (plen > sizeof s->user) return;} before Line A and \texttt{if (plen > sizeof cmd) return;} before Line C (or clamp \texttt{plen} to the destination size). Removing both overflows kills all three attacks at the root; \term{control-flow integrity} on the indirect call and guard pages between heap chunks are useful additional layers.
